extracted.intended_audience: researchers, science communicators, university press officers, and health journalists interested in accuracy of health-related press releases and news
extracted.subtask_description: Operationalizing and measuring exaggeration in academic press releases and associated news stories for health/biomedical research by comparing press-release/news claims to their associated peer-reviewed papers. Uses content analysis to quantify types of exaggeration and their association with news coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice to readers to change behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Main outcome measure: Advice to readers to change behaviour that went beyond those in the associated peer reviewed papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggeration was coded by comparing press releases/news to the associated peer-reviewed papers; 40% (95% CI 33% to 46%) of press releases contained exaggerated advice. When press releases contained such exaggeration, 58% (95% CI 48% to 68%) of news stories contained similar exaggeration, compared with 17% (10% to 24%) of news when the press releases were not exaggerated. Odds ratio for this category: 6.5 (95% CI 3.5 to 12). The study notes these rates and CIs as measures of effect; improving accuracy could reduce misleading advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal statements drawn from correlational research
rubrics_metrics.description: Main outcome measure: Presence of causal claims in press releases or news that go beyond what correlational research in the associated peer-reviewed papers supports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press releases contained exaggerated causal claims in 33% (95% CI 26% to 40%) of cases. When press releases contained such exaggeration, 81% (70% to 93%) of news stories contained similar exaggeration, compared with 18% (9% to 27%) when press releases were not exaggerated. Odds ratio: 20 (95% CI 7.6 to 51). Exaggerated causal language is operationally defined by divergence from the original paper's claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference to humans from animal research
rubrics_metrics.description: Main outcome measure: Inference to humans from non-human (animal) research that goes beyond the inferences made in the associated peer-reviewed papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 36% (95% CI 28% to 46%) of press releases contained exaggerated inference to humans from animal studies. When press releases contained such exaggeration, 86% (95% CI 77% to 95%) of news stories contained similar exaggeration, compared with 10% (0% to 19%) when press releases were not exaggerated. Odds ratio: 56 (95% CI 15 to 211). This category is coded by directly comparing the scope of inference in press releases/news to that in the academic paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: News uptake (some news uptake and mean number of stories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Outcome measures related to media uptake: the proportion of press releases with some news uptake (at least one news story) and the mean number of news stories per press release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study measured whether exaggeration in press releases affected uptake: the proportion of press releases with some news uptake and the mean number of news stories per press release were not statistically distinguishable between exaggerated and non-exaggerated press releases (error bars reported as bootstrapped 95% CIs). Figures and tables present these comparisons and associated odds ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational definition of exaggeration (comparison with associated peer-reviewed papers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exaggeration operationalized as press release or news statements that go beyond the main conclusions, advice, causal claims, or inferences presented in the associated peer-reviewed research papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification of exaggeration was done via retrospective quantitative content analysis comparing press releases (n=462) from 20 leading UK universities in 2011 and their associated peer-reviewed papers and news stories (n=668). This comparative rule (press/news claim > paper claim) is the study's core criterion for identifying exaggeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength of association reporting (odds ratios and confidence intervals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals to quantify the association between exaggeration in press releases and exaggeration in news stories for each category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper reports odds ratios and 95% CIs as primary measures of association (examples: OR=6.5 for advice-to-change-behaviour, OR=20 for causal claims, OR=56 for inference to humans from animal research). These statistics serve as the quantitative rubric for judging the strength of linkage between press-release exaggeration and news exaggeration.
